transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's a bit of a long story, but the short version is that I'm just completely overwhelmed right now. You see, over the past few weeks, or maybe it's been a month, I've just been feeling this incredible surge of creative energy. I'm an artist, you know, and usually, my process is a bit more measured, but lately, I've just been taking on everything. I mean, everything. I signed up to teach three new workshops at the community center, which sounded like a brilliant idea at the time because I had all these concepts for mixed media techniques I wanted to share. And then, while I was doing that, I decided my studio needed a complete overhaul. I started knocking down a non-load-bearing wall to get more natural light—which I'm doing myself, by the way, watching tutorials online at 3 AM because who has time to sleep when there's so much to do? 

And on top of that, I've been taking on all these new client commissions. I've been making calls, pitching ideas to galleries, just going non-stop. I thought I could handle it all, I really did. It felt like I was finally operating at my true potential, you know? But now... now I'm looking at my calendar, and I've got workshops overlapping with commission deadlines, half my studio is covered in drywall dust, and the mortgage is due next week, and I haven't actually finished any of the pieces I promised because I keep starting new ones. It's just... I've taken on far, far more than I can realistically manage, and the reality of it is all just crashing down on me. I feel like I'm suffocating under the weight of my own ideas.
You mentioned you've been watching tutorials online at 3 AM. How much sleep have you been getting lately?

Oh, sleep... gosh, how much? I honestly couldn't give you a number. It's just all a blur, really. Because, you see, the way my house is set up, my studio is right off the kitchen, so the boundaries between living space and working space are basically non-existent. I don't really transition to nighttime mode like a normal person would. 

I'll look at the clock and it's midnight, and I think, okay, I should probably wind down and make some herbal tea, but then I remember that the drywall compound needs another coat, or I get this sudden flash of inspiration for how to texture the canvas for that community center workshop I told you about. And before I know it, the birds are chirping and the sun is coming up through the skylight. 

I mean, I must be sleeping some, right? Human bodies need sleep. Sometimes I'll realize I've dozed off on the sofa with my iPad still playing those home renovation videos on my chest, but it's definitely not like I'm putting on pajamas, getting into bed, pulling up the covers, and getting a solid eight hours. It's more like... accidental micro-naps? I just haven't been keeping track of the hours at all. Time just feels completely fluid right now, just this one long continuous day, so asking me to actually quantify the sleep is... well, I just have absolutely no idea.
Have you noticed that you actually need less sleep than usual, or do you feel like you could keep going even if you don’t sleep much?

Well, that's the strange part, isn't it? You'd think with all this running around and the wall and the workshops and the pitching, I'd be absolutely exhausted. I mean, my sister called me the other day—she lives in Portland, and she's a nurse, so she's always on my case about self-care and resting and all that—and she was horrified when I told her I'd basically been awake for three days straight working on this one mixed-media collage series. She kept saying, "You must be dead on your feet, you need to go to bed right now." 

But the truth is, I don't feel tired at all! It's like my body has just decided that sleep is this completely optional thing, like an outdated software update or something that I just don't need to install anymore. I mean, usually, if I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I'm a complete zombie the next day. I can't focus, I get cranky, I can't even mix my paints properly because my eyes get all blurry. But lately? It's like I'm plugged directly into a power socket. I feel completely energized, completely wired, like I could just keep going and going and going. 

I'll be standing there at 4 AM, covered in drywall dust, and I'll think, "I should be exhausted right now," but my brain is just buzzing with a million new ideas. It's almost like the less I sleep, the more awake I feel? Which I know sounds completely contradictory and probably biologically impossible, but that's exactly how it feels. I just don't feel the need for it. It's like I've tapped into this limitless reservoir of energy that's just sustaining me, and honestly, it's thrilling, but also... maybe a little terrifying when I actually stop to think about it, which I haven't really been doing because I've been too busy working.
Have you noticed any days or periods where your mood was unusually high, excited, or irritable, along with this increased energy and activity level?

Well, it’s funny you ask about my mood, because it’s been… it’s been quite the rollercoaster, honestly. But mostly, it’s been this incredible, soaring high. I’d say for the vast majority of the days over the last month, I’ve felt so… buoyant. That’s the word for it. Just unusually buoyant and completely lit up from the inside out. 

It’s like everything in my life was finally aligning. I’d walk into the studio, even with the drywall dust everywhere, and just feel this profound sense of rightness, like the studio and my garden outside were finally clicking into place, vibrating on the exact same frequency as my soul. I’d look out the window at my hydrangeas and then look back at my canvas, and I’d just feel so elated, so full of purpose and joy that I could practically float away. I felt like I was glowing, doctor, I really did. 

But… and this is the part that’s been hard for my sister to deal with, and probably the people at the community center, too… if anyone interrupted that flow, or if they didn’t understand my vision, my mood would just flip. Like, instantly. I’d be on top of the world, and then my sister would call and ask about my invoices—because she knows I’m terrible at billing clients on time, which is true, but still—or someone would question why I was tearing down the wall, and I would just snap. I mean, sharply. I’d get so intensely irritated, almost furious, that they were dragging me down with their mundane, practical questions when I was trying to create something magnificent. 

I actually yelled at the poor guy at the hardware store because he didn't have the exact grade of sandpaper I needed for the texture I was trying to achieve. I told him he was stifling my creative process, which, looking back, is completely ridiculous, he just works in aisle four. But in the moment, any obstacle, any question about my plans, just felt like this intolerable irritation. So it’s been this mix of feeling higher and happier than I ever have, but with this really sharp, prickly edge if anyone got in my way.
Would you say that your decreased need for sleep has been a noticeable change from your usual pattern, where you genuinely don’t feel tired even after only a few hours of rest?

Well, yes, exactly like I was just saying a minute ago... it’s a complete departure from how I normally operate. Because, you see, normally—and I mean for the last, oh, almost thirty years, ever since I finished my graduate degree—I have been very, very particular about my sleep. 

When I was doing my MFA, I learned the hard way that I absolutely cannot pull all-nighters like some of the other artists could. I would try to stay up in the studio to finish a critique piece, and my lines would get sloppy, my color theory would go completely out the window, and I'd just be a weeping mess by morning. So for years and years, I've had this whole strict routine. I usually need my chamomile tea—a very specific brand, actually, the one with the little sleeping bear on the box—and I have to read for exactly thirty minutes, and I really need that solid block of seven or eight hours. If I don't get it, like I mentioned, I'm completely useless. 

So, yes, it is a massive, undeniable change. To go from needing that rigid, almost precious bedtime routine just to function as a human being, to suddenly feeling like I could run a marathon on twenty minutes of accidental couch-dozing... it’s literally night and day. I mean, my sister even pointed it out, which I already told you about, because she knows exactly how grumpy and unfocused I usually get if I even miss an hour of sleep. It's just so bizarre to not feel that heavy, behind-the-eyes exhaustion that usually hits me right around 10 PM. 

I keep waiting for the crash, you know? Like, surely my biology is going to demand payback at some point, but the invoice just hasn't arrived yet, so to speak. I just keep waiting to feel tired, but the tired just never comes, so I just keep painting and sanding and planning. It's really quite extraordinary when you think about it.
